title: Family 2: Describe your family
invitation: Now turn family words into tiny useful sentences. Describe a real family, a chosen family, a household, or a completely fictional one. The grammar should work without making you explain your private life.
summary: Practice five reusable moves: identify someone, say how many relatives you have, say who you live with, give a person's name, and compare age. Cultural mode adds the ways the two active languages handle possession, age, household language, and respectful or affectionate family labels.

blocks.title: Five sentences can do a lot
blocks.text: Start with: This is my …; I have …; I live with …; My … is named …; and My … is older/younger than me. Keep kinship and household facts separate.

blocks.title: Describing a family without defining one
blocks.text: Languages differ in how they express possession, age, respect, household membership, and family categories. A useful lesson teaches those language choices without treating any household shape as the default.

blocks.title: English examples
blocks.text: This is my sister. I have two brothers. I live with my dad and my grandmother. My cousin is named Maya. My brother is younger than me.

blocks.title: Read a family in context
blocks.text: Current Gef candidate: The Frog King, for father/daughter roles. Preferred future Family 2 book: Little Women, whose central household gives repeated sister, mother, father, age, and family-description language.

blocks.title: You can introduce the cast
blocks.description: You can describe who someone is without needing a giant family tree.
